summaries.gardner: Tesla has long been a textbook Rule Breaker: top dog and first mover in modern EVs, a visionary founder-CEO, a strong consumer brand and a stock widely called overvalued (trailing P/E about 389 in October 2026). It now fails the price-momentum trait, with the shares down about 9% over 52 weeks while the S&P 500 returned about 20%, and BYD has overtaken it in global BEV sales.
summaries.buffett: Tesla fits Buffett's approach poorly: results have been volatile (net income fell from $15.0B in 2023 to $3.8B in 2025), return on invested capital is about 5%, and the business depends on fast-changing technology. The valuation, roughly 389 times trailing earnings and about 17 times book value, leaves no margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger valued great businesses at fair prices and avoided what he could not predict; Tesla has a real brand, Supercharger network and data lead, but its auto margins collapsed from 2022 to 2025 under Chinese competition and its value rests on unproven robotaxi and Optimus bets. Its key-person dependence on Elon Musk and very high multiple would sit in his 'too hard' pile.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would classify Tesla's car business as a slowing former fast grower (revenue $97.7B in 2024, $94.8B in 2025) with a story that now depends on new ventures. With a PEG ratio around 10 and EPS down from $4.30 in 2023 to $1.08 in 2025, it fails his rule that the P/E should not exceed the growth rate, and it is anything but overlooked by Wall Street.
summaries.fisher: Tesla scores well on several Fisher points: management keeps developing new products (FSD, Megapack, Cybercab, Optimus), R&D has produced industry-leading software and manufacturing methods, and Musk takes a long-term view. It scores weaker on profit margins, which fell from a 16.8% operating margin in 2022 to about 4.6% in 2025, and on governance and candour, given repeatedly missed autonomy timelines.
summaries.graham: Tesla fails almost every Graham defensive test: it lost money until its first annual profit in 2020, has never paid a dividend, and trades at about 389 times earnings and 17 times book. Only its size and strong balance sheet ($43.5B cash and investments vs $9.3B debt in mid-2026) meet his criteria.
summaries.thiel: Tesla answers several of Thiel's seven questions well: an exceptional founder-led team, a distribution engine of its own (direct sales and Superchargers), good timing for electrification and AI, and early dominance of the premium EV niche. It is weaker on a 10x technology edge and durability, since BYD and other Chinese makers now match its cars at lower cost and Waymo leads in driverless ride-hailing.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner's 'get fit' lens stresses durable growth, cost discipline and a price that makes sense versus cash flow; Tesla's revenue declined in 2025, its free-cash-flow yield is about 0.4%, and heavy 2026 capex on AI, Cybercab and Optimus pressures cash flow. Its AI and robotics optionality fits his interest in platform shifts, but the price already assumes a great deal.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for accelerating earnings and catalysts the market has not priced; Tesla's earnings have fallen three years in a row (EPS $4.30, $2.04, $1.08 for 2023-2025) and the shares have lagged the market over the past year. Robotaxi expansion and Cybercab production are possible catalysts, but liquidity and momentum signals are not clearly in its favour today.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith requires high returns on capital, high gross margins, strong cash conversion and a sensible price; Tesla's roughly 19% gross margin, ROIC near 5% and FCF yield near 0.4% fall well short. Its brand and innovation are real, but it does not resemble the consistent compounders Fundsmith owns.
summaries.greenblatt: The Magic Formula ranks companies on high return on capital and high earnings yield; Tesla has an ROIC of about 5% and an EV/EBIT of about 340 (earnings yield under 0.3%). It would rank near the bottom of a Magic Formula screen.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs a great business, able and honest managers, and strong reinvestment opportunities; Tesla has large reinvestment opportunities and an owner-operator CEO with a large stake (insiders own about 28.5%), but its current returns on capital are low and governance is contested. The business leg is weakened by falling auto margins.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach seeks simple, low-risk businesses bought at a deep discount; Tesla is complex, priced at about 389 times trailing earnings, and its value depends on uncertain new ventures. It is close to the opposite of a 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' bet.
summaries.wood: Tesla is a central fit for Cathie Wood's disruptive-innovation framework: it combines EVs, battery energy storage, autonomous driving AI and humanoid robotics, platforms ARK has long highlighted. Falling battery costs, Cybercab production in 2026 and robotaxi services in several US cities support the thesis, though auto margins and deliveries have weakened.
summaries.ackman: Ackman prefers simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with strong balance sheets and moats, bought at a discount; Tesla has the balance sheet and brand but not the predictability, with operating income falling from $13.7B in 2022 to $4.4B in 2025. Its very high valuation leaves no discount to intrinsic value.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep favoured 'scale economies shared' businesses that pass savings to customers; Tesla has done some of this through repeated price cuts and cheaper 'Standard' trims as costs fell. But its scale advantage has been matched or exceeded by BYD (4.6M NEVs in 2025 vs Tesla's 1.64M deliveries), so the flywheel is not clearly strengthening.
summaries.valentine: Don Valentine backed big markets and products solving painful problems; Tesla addresses huge markets in transport, grid storage and potentially robotics, and was built by an exceptional founder. As a mature public company with a $1T-plus market value, the early-stage upside Valentine sought is largely priced in.
summaries.nash: Tesla is one of Tom Nash's own examples of a company the market misreads, and it passes his trend, sanity-check and balance-sheet steps with $43.5B of cash against $16.1B of debt. It fails many of his numbers tests: trailing operating margin is 4.13%, revenue growth plus FCF margin is about 17, free cash flow was negative in Q2 2026 and it missed EPS estimates in two of the last four quarters. Its valuation (forward P/E of 191, PEG of 10.19) and a bear-case DCF of about $27 a share are far from his buy zone.

momentum.evidence: TSLA fell about 9.3% over the 52 weeks to October 13, 2026 (to $375.23), while the S&P 500 (SPY) returned about 20.4% over the past year.

g4.evidence: Tesla is led by co-founder Elon Musk and has a high-profile shareholder base and partners, and Musk bought about $1 billion of Tesla shares in September 2025.

g6.evidence: Many analysts call the stock overvalued, e.g. UBS reiterated a Sell in January 2026 and JPMorgan cut its target to $145 in January 2026, with the trailing P/E near 389.

simple.evidence: Car and battery sales are easy to understand, but much of the valuation rests on hard-to-judge AI bets such as unsupervised FSD, robotaxis and the Optimus robot.

b2.evidence: Tesla only turned its first annual profit in 2020, and net income has since swung from $15.0B in 2023 to $7.1B in 2024 and $3.8B in 2025.

integrity.evidence: Musk owns a large stake and his 2025 award is tied to reaching an $8.5 trillion market value, but repeatedly missed FSD timelines and concerns about board independence weigh on candour and governance.

b6.evidence: Tesla avoids copying peers and pursues its own path in direct sales and camera-only autonomy, but it has expanded into many ambitious new ventures (Semi, Cybercab, Optimus, AI chips) at the same time.

roic.evidence: Return on invested capital is about 5.5% and return on equity about 4.7% on a trailing basis (StockAnalysis, October 2026), down sharply from 2022-2023.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow of $6.2B in 2025 exceeded net income of $3.8B, but it was only $3.6B in 2024 and heavy AI and factory capex is expected to pressure it in 2026.

b10.evidence: Tesla has never paid a dividend and reinvested everything, and its market value (about $1.3 trillion at $375.23 per share) far exceeds the cumulative earnings it has retained.

safety.evidence: At about 389 times trailing earnings and 17 times book value, the price is far above any conservative estimate of value based on current earnings or assets.

fairprice.evidence: A PEG ratio of about 10 and a forward P/E of about 191 are hard to justify given that revenue fell in 2025 and EPS fell to $1.08.

mu5.evidence: Tesla could be hurt by cheaper Chinese EVs, Waymo's lead in robotaxis, safety incidents or regulation slowing FSD, brand damage linked to Musk, and key-person risk.

reinvest.evidence: Tesla has large reinvestment opportunities in Cybercab, Optimus, Semi and energy storage, but its current returns on capital are only about 5%, so high returns are unproven.

ly2.evidence: The car business looks like a slowing former fast grower, while the investment story now depends on robotaxis and robots, which makes the category unclear.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E is about 389 while EPS fell from $4.30 in 2023 to $1.08 in 2025, giving a PEG ratio of about 10.

runway.evidence: Energy storage, FSD subscriptions (about 1.48M in Q2 2026) and robotaxis offer new growth, but vehicle revenue fell in 2025 and consensus expects about 13% growth in 2026.

ly7.evidence: Apart from Musk's roughly $1 billion purchase in September 2025, insiders have mostly been sellers, and the share count rose about 0.6% over the past year.

ly8.evidence: Tesla is one of the most widely followed and debated stocks on Wall Street, covered by more than 40 analysts.

fi2.evidence: As the Model 3 and Model Y matured, Tesla launched Cybertruck, Megapack, FSD subscriptions, and started Cybercab production and Optimus development in 2026.

fi3.evidence: Its R&D produced FSD v13/v14 (widely seen as the most capable consumer driver-assistance system), gigacasting, in-house AI chips and a leading grid-battery business (46.7 GWh deployed in 2025).

fi4.evidence: Tesla sells directly with almost no traditional advertising, but deliveries fell from 1.81M in 2023 to about 1.64M in 2025 despite repeated price cuts.

longterm.evidence: Management has accepted sharply lower margins and heavy capex to invest in autonomy, AI compute and robotics, following Musk's multi-decade Master Plans.

gr1.evidence: Tesla had $94.8B of revenue in 2025 and a market value of about $1.3 trillion in October 2026.

ni10.evidence: Tesla lost $862M in 2019 and only reported its first annual profit ($721M) in 2020, so it was not profitable in each of the last ten years.

gr4.evidence: Tesla has never paid a dividend.

eps10.evidence: EPS rose from losses in the mid-2010s to $1.08 in 2025, but it has fallen 75% from $4.30 in 2023, so the gain rests on a weak recent base.

gr6.evidence: The average of 2023-2025 EPS ($4.30, $2.04, $1.08) is about $2.47, so the $375.23 price is roughly 150 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: A P/E of about 389 times a P/B of about 17.1 gives a product of over 6,600, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Tesla's fleet-trained FSD and manufacturing methods are leading, but no single technology is ten times better than rivals such as BYD's batteries or Waymo's driverless system.

timing.evidence: The timing for AI-driven autonomy and grid storage looks right, but the US EV tax credit ended on September 30, 2025 and EV demand has slowed in key markets.

th3.evidence: Tesla began with the small premium EV niche (Roadster, then Model S) and expanded into mass-market cars, energy storage and robotaxis.

team.evidence: Founder-level CEO Elon Musk has built Tesla and SpaceX into industry leaders, though several senior AI, Optimus and sales executives left in 2024-2026.

th5.evidence: Tesla sells directly online and through its own stores and runs its own Supercharger network of over 70,000 connectors, bypassing dealers.

durable.evidence: Its brand, data and energy business may endure, but its global BEV share fell from about 16.5% in 2024 to 11.9% in 2025 as Chinese rivals advanced.

th7.evidence: Tesla saw the mass EV opportunity early, but most automakers and many Chinese firms now pursue the same EV, autonomy and humanoid-robot opportunities.

trend.evidence: Tesla is a leading player in vehicle electrification, grid battery storage and AI-driven autonomy, with about 1.48M FSD subscriptions in Q2 2026.

dr1.evidence: EPS has fallen three years running ($4.30 in 2023, $2.04 in 2024, $1.08 in 2025), and analysts such as JPMorgan cut targets in early 2026.

dr2.evidence: Robotaxi expansion, Cybercab production and energy growth could improve results, but heavy capex and auto price competition make this uncertain.

dr4.evidence: Lower rates help car financing, but the end of the US EV tax credit, looser emissions rules (less regulatory-credit revenue) and tariffs work against it.

dr6.evidence: Identifiable catalysts include Cybercab volume production, expansion of driverless robotaxi service to more cities, Semi production in Nevada and Optimus milestones.

dr7.evidence: Falling earnings, a trailing P/E near 389 and dependence on unproven ventures make a large concentrated position hard to justify on fundamentals.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was about 18-19% (18.85% trailing), low compared with software or luxury goods and down from 25.6% in 2022.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of $5.76B against a market value of about $1.3 trillion gives an FCF yield of about 0.4%.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 340, an earnings yield on enterprise value of under 0.3%.

pa2.evidence: Brand damage and the loss of EV tax credits may be temporary, but competition from cheaper Chinese EVs looks structural.

pa4.evidence: With the share price far above the value implied by current earnings, a failure of the robotaxi or robot bets could cause large, lasting losses.

wo1.evidence: Tesla is a leader in AI (FSD, robotaxis), robotics (Optimus) and energy storage (Megapack, 46.7 GWh deployed in 2025).

wo2.evidence: Battery and vehicle costs have fallen with scale, enabling repeated price cuts and cheaper 'Standard' Model 3 and Y trims in late 2025.

wo3.evidence: Tesla combines EVs, battery storage, autonomous driving AI and humanoid robotics in one company.

wo4.evidence: Robotaxi and humanoid-robot markets could be many times larger than today's auto revenue if they work, but that is unproven within five years.

ac3.evidence: Car demand is sensitive to interest rates and tax credits, and costs depend on lithium, battery materials and tariffs (energy margin fell to about 20% in Q2 2026 partly due to tariffs).

ns1.evidence: Tesla has passed cost savings to buyers through price cuts from 2023 to 2025, but this was partly forced by competition and BYD has a similar or lower cost base.

ns4.evidence: Success in autonomy and robotics could make it much stronger, but its share of the core EV market is falling, so a stronger position is not clear.

va2.evidence: Tesla tackles large problems: transport emissions, grid reliability through battery storage, and road safety and cost through autonomous driving.

tn1.evidence: Tesla was founded in 2003 to build electric vehicles and now sells into electrification, grid battery storage and AI autonomy, with about 1.48M FSD subscriptions in Q2 2026.

tn2.evidence: Nash cites Tesla as a company the market sees as a car maker while it becomes an AI, robotics and energy business, but at 383 times trailing earnings the market already prices much of that story.

tn3.evidence: It is a $1.46T US company founded in 2003, outside Nash's avoid zones, though car sales are cyclical.

tn4.evidence: It is profitable (trailing net income $3,806M) and has more cash ($43,524M) than debt ($16,080M), though revenue fell 2.93% in FY2025 before trailing revenue rose 11.76%.

tn5.evidence: Cash exceeded debt in each of the last six quarters, but free cash flow was negative at -$1,092M in Q2 2026 as capital spending rose to $5,789M.

tn6.evidence: Trailing revenue grew 11.76% to $103,619M, but FY2025 revenue fell 2.93% and FY2024 grew only 0.95%.

tn7.evidence: Trailing revenue growth of 11.76% plus a free-cash-flow margin of 5.56% gives about 17.3, well below 40.

tn8.evidence: In FY2025 operating expenses (gross profit minus operating income) rose 30.1% to $12,739M while revenue fell 2.93%, and trailing operating income fell to $4,278M.

tn9.evidence: It fails at least two instant kills: a 4.13% trailing operating margin, far below 20%, and EPS misses in two of the last four quarters (Q3 2025 and Q2 2026).

tn10.evidence: Tesla faces NHTSA investigations into FSD and Autopilot, a California DMV case over Autopilot marketing and wrongful-death lawsuits such as the $243M Florida verdict in August 2025.

tn11.evidence: It sells electric cars, battery storage and FSD software that help drivers and utilities move to clean energy, charging per vehicle, per system and by subscription, but the robotaxi and Optimus story it is valued on is not yet a clear revenue model.

tn13.evidence: Scorecard total 70 of 130: cash vs debt 10, revenue growth 5, operating margin 0, short interest 10, institutional ownership (43.1%) 5, revenue faster than expenses 0, 5-year return (+38.8% vs SPY's +91.1%) 0, moat 5, CEO 10, recession-proof pricing power 0, secular trend 10, culture and mission 10, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue fell in FY2025, operating margin dropped from 16.81% in FY2022 to 4.59% in FY2025 and free cash flow fell from $7,561M to $3,581M before recovering to $6,220M, though cash exceeded debt every year.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is 12.81x, assets of $148,524M are 2.43x liabilities of $61,005M, the current ratio is 1.94 and liabilities are 0.70x equity.

tn18.evidence: Elon Musk has led Tesla since 2008, counts as a co-founder and bought about $1B of shares in September 2025, but operating margin has fallen from 16.81% in FY2022 to 4.13% and FSD timelines have repeatedly slipped.

tn20.evidence: Tesla missed EPS consensus in Q2 2026 ($0.33 vs $0.53) and in Q3 2025, beating in only two of the last four quarters.

tn21.evidence: Operating margins have declined for three years, other insiders such as Kimbal Musk and chair Robyn Denholm have sold shares, and Musk's political and social-media controversies are a governance red flag.

tn22.evidence: It has $103,619M of trailing revenue and no regular share sales, but fundamentals are weakening and the stock is driven by nonstop media hype around robotaxis and Optimus.

tn24.evidence: At $375.23, a 10% discount rate, a 4.9% FCF margin and 4% terminal growth imply about 84% annual revenue growth for five years, far above the 11.76% it is delivering.

tn25.evidence: With 3-year average growth of 5.6% trimmed to 4.5%, a 4.9% FCF margin, 4% terminal growth, a 12% discount rate and net cash of $27,444M, value is about $27 per share, far below $375.23.

tn26.evidence: A forward P/E of 191.22 and a PEG of 10.19 (StockAnalysis) are far above car and tech peers and the 1.0 PEG limit.
